title: Describing people
description: Describe how people look and what they're like with tragen and aussehen, and learn adjective endings after der, die, das. Then find people at a party.

grammarNotes.title: Describing someone: sein, aussehen, tragen
grammarNotes.body:
Three verbs do most of the work:

- **sein** for size, build and hair: *Er ist groß. Seine Haare sind kurz.*
- **aussehen** (to look) for the impression someone gives: *Er sieht nett aus.*
- **tragen** (to wear) for glasses, a beard and clothes: *Sie trägt eine Brille.*

After *sein* and *aussehen*, the adjective has **no ending**, just like in Unit 10.

**die Haare** is plural, so use *sind*. For people, **groß** means *tall* and **klein** means *short*. **kurz** is for things like hair.

You'll often hear *Er hat kurze Haare* (He has short hair). With no *der/die/das* in front, the ending works differently: learn it as a chunk for now.
table: Seine Haare sind kurz und blond.
Er ist groß. / Sie ist klein.

grammarNotes.title: tragen and aussehen
grammarNotes.body:
**tragen** (to wear, to carry) changes **a → ä** in the *du* and *er / sie / es* forms, like *fahren*.

**aussehen** (to look) is separable, and changes **e → ie** like *sehen*. The *aus* goes to the end, and the adjective goes just before it: *Du **siehst** heute toll **aus**.* After a modal verb it stays in one piece: *Ich möchte gut **aussehen**.*

Two words to watch:

- **sympathisch** is a false friend. It means *likeable*, not *sympathetic*.
- **dick** is as direct as English *fat*. The friendly word is **schlank** (slim).

grammarNotes.title: Adjectives before a noun: der nette Mann
grammarNotes.body:
After *sein*, an adjective has no ending: *Der Mann ist nett.*

When the adjective goes **before** the noun, it needs an ending. After **der, die, das** in the subject form (the **nominative**: the person or thing doing the action), the ending is always **-e**:

- *der nett**e** Mann*
- *die nett**e** Frau*
- *das nett**e** Kind*

**dieser** and **welcher** work the same way: *dieser groß**e** Mann, welches klein**e** Kind*.

Now colours can go before a noun too: *Der rot**e** Mantel ist schön.* After *ein* and *eine* the endings are different; that comes in Unit 23.

grammarNotes.title: -e or -en? The whole table
grammarNotes.body:
After **der, die, das** (and *dieser, welcher*), an adjective before a noun ends in **-e** or **-en**. Nothing else!

- 🟩 **-e** in five places: all three singular subjects, plus *die* and *das* words as objects (they don't change in the object form).
- 🟦 **-en** everywhere else: *der* words as objects (*den*), the whole dative (after *mit, zu, in*), and all plurals.

Quick check: after **den** or **dem**, after *mit der*, and with any plural, it's always **-en**.

grammarNotes.title: Leute, Menschen and the dative plural
grammarNotes.body:
Both words mean *people*:

- **die Leute** is the everyday word for a group of people. It only exists in the plural: *Die Leute hier sind nett.*
- **der Mensch** is a human being. The plural **die Menschen** is for people in general and sounds a little more serious: *In Berlin wohnen viele Menschen.*

In conversation, *Leute* is usually the one you want.

In the **dative plural** (after *mit, zu, in*), the article is **den** and the noun adds **-n** if it can: *mit den Kinder**n***. Nouns that already end in *-n* or in *-s* stay as they are: *mit den Frauen, mit den Fotos*. German uses **mit** where English says *with* or *in*: *der Mann mit dem Hut* = the man in the hat.

exercises.title: die Haare: hair
exercises.body:
Time to describe people! Start with hair. **das Haar** is one single hair, so for the hair on your head Germans use the plural: **die Haare**.

Because it's plural, use **sind**: *Seine Haare **sind** kurz.*

- **lang** = long
- **kurz** = short
- **blond** = blond
- **lockig** = curly

You also know *dunkel, braun, schwarz, grau* and *rot*. After *sind*, adjectives have no ending, just like in Unit 10.

examples.text: Seine Haare sind kurz und dunkel.
examples.translation: His hair is short and dark.

exercises.title: Tall, short, slim
exercises.body:
For someone's height and build:

- **groß** = tall. For people, *groß* means tall, not big.
- **klein** = short (for people). Use *kurz* for things like hair.
- **schlank** = slim
- **dünn** = thin
- **dick** = fat

*dick* is as direct as English *fat*, so be careful saying it about someone. *schlank* is the friendly, positive word. For things, *dick* just means *thick*.

examples.text: Mein Bruder ist groß und schlank.
examples.translation: My brother is tall and slim.

exercises.title: hübsch and ziemlich
exercises.body:
- **hübsch** = pretty. Use it for women, girls, children and things.
- **ziemlich** = quite, rather. It goes before the adjective, just like *sehr*.

From weak to strong: *nicht so groß → ziemlich groß → sehr groß*.

exercises.title: tragen: to wear
exercises.body:
**tragen** means to wear (and also to carry). It changes its vowel like *fahren*: **a → ä** in the *du* and *er / sie / es* forms.

- ich trage
- du **trägst**
- er / sie / es **trägt**
- wir tragen

What you wear is the object, so *der* words take **den** or **einen**: *Er trägt **einen** Mantel.*

accepted: trägt
exercises.translation: He's wearing a coat today.

exercises.instruction: Which form fits? Du ___ heute eine Jacke.

exercises.title: Brille, Bart, Glatze
exercises.body:
- **die Brille** = glasses. It's singular in German: *eine Brille* is one pair of glasses. You *wear* it: *Sie trägt eine Brille.*
- **der Bart** = the beard. You can *wear* a beard too: *Er trägt einen Bart.* *Er hat einen Bart* is also fine.
- **die Glatze** = a bald head. *Er hat eine Glatze.* = He's bald.

exercises.translation: Does your father wear glasses?

exercises.title: aussehen: to look
exercises.body:
To say how someone **looks**, use **aussehen**. It's separable, and it changes its vowel like *sehen*: *er **sieht** … **aus***.

- **Wie sieht er aus?** = What does he look like?
- *Er sieht müde aus.* = He looks tired.

The adjective goes just before *aus*, and like after *sein*, it has **no ending**. To ask what someone is like as a person, say **Wie ist er?**

exercises.title: What are they like?
exercises.body:
To ask what someone is like as a person, say **Wie ist er?** or **Wie ist sie?**

- **nett** = nice, kind
- **freundlich** = friendly
- **lustig** = funny, fun
- **ernst** = serious
- **schüchtern** = shy

You already know **ruhig** (quiet) and **laut** (loud) too.

examples.text: Er ist lustig und ziemlich laut.
Meine Schwester ist ruhig und ein bisschen schüchtern.
examples.translation: My sister is quiet and a bit shy.

exercises.title: sympathisch: a false friend
exercises.body:
**sympathisch** does *not* mean sympathetic. It means **likeable**: someone you like straight away.

*Er ist sehr sympathisch.* = He's really likeable. / I really like him.

Put **un-** in front for the opposite: *unsympathisch* = not likeable, *unfreundlich* = unfriendly.

exercises.title: Before a noun: der nette Mann
exercises.body:
So far, adjectives came **after** the noun, with *sein* or *aussehen*, and had no ending: *Der Mann ist nett.*

When an adjective goes **before** a noun, it needs an ending. After **der, die, das**, in the subject form (the **nominative**: the person doing the action), it's always **-e**:

- **der** nett**e** Mann
- **die** nett**e** Frau
- **das** nett**e** Kind

One ending for all three genders!

exercises.title: das Mädchen, dieser and welcher
exercises.body:
**das Mädchen** = the girl. Words ending in **-chen** are always *das*, even for a girl.

**dieser** (this) and **welcher** (which) work just like *der, die, das*, so the adjective after them ends in **-e** too:

- *dies**er** groß**e** Mann*
- *welch**es** klein**e** Mädchen*

And now colours can go before the noun: *Der rot**e** Mantel ist schön.*

exercises.title: kennen: to know someone
exercises.body:
**kennen** = to know a person or a place, to be familiar with it. It's regular: *ich kenne, du kennst, er kennt*.

The person you know is the **object**, so *der* becomes **den**: *Ich kenne **den** Mann.*

exercises.title: The object: den großen Mann
exercises.body:
When a *der* word is the object, **der → den**. The adjective changes too: **-e → -en**.

- *Der groß**e** Mann ist hier.* (subject)
- *Kennst du **den** groß**en** Mann?* (object)

*die* and *das* words don't change in the object form, so they keep **-e**:

- *Ich kenne **die** nett**e** Frau.*
- *Ich kenne **das** klein**e** Kind.*

Easy to remember: after **den**, it's **-en**.

examples.translation: Do you know the tall man?

accepted: großen
exercises.translation: Do you know the tall man?

exercises.title: Colours and clothes
exercises.body:
In Unit 11, colours could only go after *ist*. Now they can go before the noun, with the same endings. Clothes after **tragen** are objects, so watch the *der* words:

- *Der rot**e** Mantel ist schön.* (subject)
- *Sie trägt **den** rot**en** Mantel.* (object)

examples.text: Der graue Mantel ist zu teuer.
examples.translation: The grey coat is too expensive.

accepted: blauen
exercises.translation: He's wearing the blue jumper.

exercises.title: Plural and dative: always -en
exercises.body:
Two more places, and both are easy: the ending is **always -en**.

- **Plural**: *die nett**en** Kinder*
- **Dative**, after *mit, zu, in*: *mit dem nett**en** Mann, mit der nett**en** Frau, mit dem nett**en** Kind*

In the dative plural, the article is **den** and the noun adds **-n**: *mit den Haare**n***.

So the whole rule: 🟩 **-e** after *der, die, das* as the subject, and after *die, das* as the object. 🟦 **-en** everywhere else.

Both mean *people*:

- **der Mensch** is a human being. The plural **die Menschen** is for people in general and sounds a bit more serious: *In Berlin wohnen viele Menschen.*

In conversation, *Leute* is usually the one you want. Both are plural, so the adjective ends in **-en**: *die nett**en** Leute*.

exercises.title: Finding someone
exercises.body:
- **da drüben** = over there
- **der Hut** = the hat

To pick someone out, German uses **mit** where English often says *in* or *with*: *der Mann **mit dem** Hut* = the man in the hat, *die Frau **mit der** Brille* = the woman with glasses. After *mit* comes the dative, so adjectives end in **-en**.

**auf der Party** = at the party.
